recipe.history:
Pulled pork is one of the defining dishes of American barbecue, with roots that run deep into the foodways of the American South and further back into the Caribbean and West African cooking traditions that shaped Southern cuisine. The word 'barbecue' itself derives from the Taíno word 'barbacoa,' referring to a wooden framework used to slow-cook meat over low heat, and Spanish explorers documented the technique across the Caribbean and Central America in the 16th century. West African enslaved people in the American South brought with them a deep knowledge of low-and-slow cooking, the use of whole animal butchery, and the transformative power of smoke, and it was the confluence of these traditions with the pork-heavy diet of the colonial South that produced the regional barbecue styles we know today: the vinegar-based whole hog tradition of the Carolinas, the tomato and molasses-based Kansas City style, the dry-rub tradition of Memphis. Pulled pork — the slow-cooked, shredded shoulder of a pig, rendered tender by hours of low heat until the collagen melts into gelatin and the muscle falls apart — is the foundational preparation in all of these traditions.

Pulled pork's arrival on sliders, as opposed to full-size sandwiches, reflects a broader American shift toward shareable, snackable food formats in the 2010s, driven by the rise of sports bar culture, game night entertaining, and the slider's intrinsic logic as a vehicle for bold, saucy fillings. A pulled pork slider offered something a full sandwich did not: you could eat two or three of them in the same time it took to work through one big sandwich, and because each slider was a complete unit with its own bun-to-filling ratio, every bite was proportional. Adding nacho cheese sauce to the pulled pork slider was an act of pure American excess that turned out to be an act of culinary genius — the sharp, salty, oozing processed cheese cutting through the pork's smoky sweetness and the pickle's brine in a way that made the whole thing irresistible and impossible to stop eating, which is exactly what you want at a card game.

Card game night food is a specific genre with specific requirements: it must be handleable with one hand so the other hand stays on your cards, it must be flavorful enough to be worth eating between hands, it must be communal rather than precious, and it must be the kind of food that causes no regret at midnight when the game is still going. Pulled pork sliders with nacho cheese and pickle chips satisfy every one of these requirements. I discovered this at a poker night years ago when I brought a batch on a whim, and within twenty minutes two people had asked to be dealt out so they could make seconds. The cards sat on the table. No one minded.

The beef patty base of these sliders — yes, there is a small beef patty beneath the pulled pork for structural integrity and additional richness — must be cooked to medium rare: 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit, 54 to 57 Celsius. This is not negotiable. The pulled pork is slow-cooked fully through, the nacho cheese is fully cooked, the pickle is cured — but the beef patty is the one element in this slider where temperature precision matters, and pulling it at medium rare ensures that the burger beneath the pork is juicy enough to complement rather than merely support the toppings. Medium rare beef at the base of a loaded slider is the structural and flavorful anchor. Cook it right.
ingredients: 1 egg beaten with 1 tbsp water (egg wash)
2 large dill pickles, sliced into 1/4-inch rounds
instructions: 1. Make the pulled pork (start at least 6 hours ahead, or the day before): Preheat oven to 300°F (150°C). Combine all dry spices and salt and rub the pork shoulder all over. Place in a Dutch oven, add apple cider vinegar and stock, cover tightly, and braise in the oven for 4 to 5 hours until the meat is pull-apart tender and registers 200°F (93°C) internally. Remove from oven and let rest 30 minutes. Pull the pork into shreds using two forks, discarding the bone and any large fat pieces. Reserve the braising liquid.
2. Make the BBQ sauce: Combine all sauce ingredients in a saucepan over medium heat. Simmer 10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until thickened slightly. Season to taste.
3. Toss the pulled pork with half the BBQ sauce and a few tablespoons of the reserved braising liquid. Keep warm.

4. Make the slider buns: Combine warm milk, yeast, and sugar in a stand mixer bowl. Let stand 5 minutes until foamy. Add flour, salt, egg, and butter. Knead with dough hook on medium for 8 minutes until smooth. Transfer to an oiled bowl, cover, and rise 1 to 1.5 hours until doubled. Divide into 12 equal portions, shape into smooth balls, arrange in a 9x13-inch pan, cover, and proof 40 minutes. Preheat oven to 375°F (190°C). Brush with egg wash and bake 14 to 16 minutes until golden. Pull apart before using.

5. Make the nacho cheese sauce: Melt butter in a saucepan over medium heat. Whisk in flour and cook 1 minute. Gradually whisk in milk. Cook, whisking constantly, until the mixture thickens, about 3 to 4 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in grated cheddar and American cheese until fully melted and smooth. Add garlic powder, cumin, cayenne, and salt. Keep warm over very low heat, stirring occasionally.

6. Shape the slider beef patties: Season ground beef with salt, black pepper, and garlic powder. Divide into 12 equal portions. Shape into small patties roughly 1/2 inch thick and slightly wider than the slider buns.

7. Heat a cast iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Add a thin film of neutral oil. Working in batches, cook slider patties undisturbed 2 minutes, flip, and cook 1 to 2 more minutes. Remove at 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C) for medium rare. Tent with foil and rest 2 minutes.
8. Toast slider buns cut-side down in the skillet for 30 to 45 seconds until lightly golden.

9. Assemble: Spread a thin layer of BBQ sauce on the bottom bun. Place the medium rare beef patty on the bottom bun. Pile a generous mound of BBQ-sauced pulled pork on the patty. Add 3 to 4 pickle chips. Drizzle nacho cheese sauce generously over the top. Close the bun and serve immediately with extra nacho cheese sauce and BBQ sauce on the side.
